title: Personal identity
examples: If I lose all my memories, am I still me?
Does changing my body parts change who I am?
What makes me the same person over time?

explain.say: Today we explore what makes you you. We consider the idea of personal identity.

draw.text: Personal Identity: What makes you you?

explain.say: First we look at the famous ship of Theseus puzzle. It questions what makes something the same.
Imagine a ship where every single plank is replaced over time. Is it still the same ship?
Next we consider memory and the self. Our memories seem very important to who we think we are.
If someone could perfectly implant all your memories into a new body, would you still be you?
In everyday life, think about learning a new skill like riding a bike. You change, but you are still you.

faq.q: If I lose all my memories, am I still the same person?
faq.a: Philosophically, this is debated. Some argue that memories are key to identity, while others point to something else.
asks: If I forget everything, who am I?

faq.q: Does replacing all my body parts change who I am?
faq.a: The ship puzzle suggests that mere physical replacement might not break identity, but it is a deep question.
asks: If I grow old, am I still me?

faq.q: Is my consciousness the most important part of my identity?
faq.a: Many philosophers focus on consciousness, suggesting it is the continuous stream of awareness that matters most.
asks: Is thinking enough to keep me 'me'?
What is the core of my self?

faq.q: How do philosophers solve the ship of Theseus problem?
faq.a: There is no single agreed-upon answer. Some focus on continuity, others on structure.
asks: What is the right answer for the ship?
Is there a rule for identity?

faq.q: Does my personal identity change when I grow up?
faq.a: Yes, because our beliefs and experiences change, our understanding of self evolves over time.
asks: Am I a different person now?

facts: The Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment about identity.
Personal identity concerns what makes a person the same over time.
Memory is often cited as a major component of personal identity.
The concept challenges whether physical continuity or psychological continuity is more important.
